articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia. The agency also published amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on these changes.
These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes and specific activities in the targeted regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on five China-based entities for trade-secret theft, support for that theft, or links to MiraclePlus. These entities include BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (also known as MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I) and SHANGHAI ZHISUAN TECHNOLOGY CO LTD.

The designations include blocking of property and restrictions on loans from U.S. financial institutions, foreign exchange transactions, and banking transactions, with an exception for the importation of goods. OFAC also issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing certain transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind-down of transactions involving certain blocked entities until January 19, 2027.

The State Department also announced these sanctions, which target entities connected to PRC national Linwei Ding. The actions aim to protect American intellectual property and address cyber-related threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Venezuela-related General License 60A, titled "Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela." This amended general license replaces and supersedes the previous General License 60.

The new General License 60A extends the authorization period for earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela, which was originally set to expire on October 23, 2026, until April 21, 2027. This extension aims to facilitate continued humanitarian aid to the region.
In conjunction with the amended general license, OFAC also updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) 1263 to reflect the extended authorization end date.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Designates Cuban Entity, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 15, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to target Iran's international financial networks and shadow banking architecture.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also designated a Cuban entity, Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a state-owned bank. This designation is part of broader sanctions against Cuba.
Furthermore, OFAC issued new and amended general licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on these recent designations and to clarify authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez from SDN List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez, the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This action lifts asset-blocking restrictions and allows U.S. persons to engage in transactions with him that were previously prohibited.

Rodríguez, who has served as the head of Venezuela's legislature since 2021, was originally designated in September 2018 under Executive Order 13692 for being an official of the Venezuelan government. The removal covers five separate entries associated with Rodríguez, including variations of his name.

While OFAC did not publicly explain the reason for the removal, it comes amid continued scrutiny of Washington's economic restrictions on Venezuela and follows the removal of his sister, Delcy Rodríguez, in April 2026. Despite the delisting, Canada still lists him under its Venezuela regulations, and a separate U.S. visa restriction reportedly remains in place.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt illicit networks.

Specifically, OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against four individuals and 11 entities in Mexico for supporting Cartel del Noreste through businesses involved in horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector.
These designations aim to sever financial ties and limit the operational capabilities of criminal organizations that pose a threat to U.S. national security.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs. These violations involved approximately $14.83 million in transactions across sanctions targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma (Myanmar), Somalia, narcotics trafficking, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, stemmed from deficiencies in payment screening, delayed sanctions watchlist updates, weaknesses in alert prioritization, and human errors related to accounts associated with blocked individuals. The largest category of violations involved 403 transactions, totaling $14.34 million, routed through 35 sanctioned banks, including 32 Russian banks, two Belarusian banks, and one Iranian bank.

OFAC determined that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation. This settlement was announced alongside broader Treasury enforcement actions against Bank of America, totaling over $1.21 billion in penalties for sanctions and anti-money laundering compliance failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 Over Sanctions and Reporting Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations. The settlement addresses four apparent violations of dealing in blocked property and six apparent violations related to an incomplete response to an OFAC subpoena.

The violations occurred between September 2023 and February 2024, when Pegasus facilitated the importation of a packet-filling machine from Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., a Chinese supplier designated under Executive Order 14059 for selling pill presses to counterfeit-pill makers. Pegasus failed to identify the designated company due to deficiencies in its compliance review and program, and also initially failed to respond fully to an OFAC administrative subpoena for six months.

OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The settlement amount reflects consideration of aggravating factors, including reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions requirements, and mitigating factors such as no prior enforcement history, the company's small size, and extensive remedial commitments.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New General License Authorizing Russian Diesel Fuel Imports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Russia-related General License (GL) 135, titled "Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin." This general license temporarily authorizes certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.

The issuance of GL 135 follows an announcement by President Trump that the U.S. reached a deal with Russia to immediately release 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to global markets, with additional amounts to follow. This move comes amidst rising diesel prices worldwide and appears to be a response to global energy market conditions.

However, the authorization faces legal uncertainty and has drawn criticism from a bipartisan group of senators who argue it may violate the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act. GL 135 does not authorize debits to accounts of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund of the Russian Federation, or the Ministry of Finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These designations are part of ongoing efforts to address threats emanating from Iran.

In addition to the new designations, OFAC issued an Iran-related General License to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions. The details of this general license aim to mitigate unintended consequences of the sanctions.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions policies concerning the Russian Federation. This amendment seeks to refine the scope of authorized activities under the Russia sanctions program.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty stems from 475 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs, involving approximately $14.83 million in transactions.

The violations occurred between September 2021 and April 2025 and involved processing payments through blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for sanctioned individuals, delays in updating watchlists, and mishandling accounts associated with blocked persons. The sanctions programs implicated include those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to no reduction in the base penalty. This penalty is part of a larger set of enforcement actions by the U.S. Treasury Department against Bank of America, totaling over $1.21 billion, for anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Sanctions and Reporting Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $175,015 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The penalty addresses four apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and six apparent violations of the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

The violations involved facilitating the importation of a machine from a designated Chinese supplier and failing to fully respond to an OFAC administrative subpoena for six months. OFAC determined that the conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's consideration of various factors, including the company's reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions requirements and its subsequent remedial measures. This action highlights the significant sanctions risks faced by logistics and freight forwarding companies.

articles.headline: Global Markets React to U.S. Outbound Investment Rule and Russia Sanctions Waivers
body: Global markets are closely watching the implications of the U.S. Treasury Department's proposed rule under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act (COINS Act), which outlines restrictions on U.S. investments in certain technology sectors in countries like China, Russia, Cuba, Iran, and North Korea. While Venezuela was notably omitted from the list of 'countries of concern,' the rule still requires notification for investments in six technology areas and imposes a total ban on artificial intelligence investments in the targeted nations.

Simultaneously, President Trump's recent executive order, which waives most of the new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, has introduced a degree of uncertainty. This waiver, issued less than a month after the Act was signed into law, effectively returns U.S. Russia-related sanctions to their pre-Act status quo, with the exception of Iran-related sections.

The temporary authorization of Russian-origin diesel fuel imports through April 2027, also enacted by OFAC, has been met with mixed reactions, with some experts doubting its substantial impact on global diesel prices and a bipartisan group of senators questioning its legality. These developments create a complex environment for international trade and investment, particularly in energy and technology sectors.

articles.headline: EU and Australia Impose New Sanctions on North Korea Over Weapons Programs and Russia Ties
body: The European Union Council has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to North Korea's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions. The European Council strongly condemned the deployment of DPRK military forces in Russia's war against Ukraine and the continued military support provided by North Korea, Iran, and Belarus to Russia.

In a coordinated effort, the Australian Government has also imposed targeted financial sanctions and travel bans on two individuals and two entities involved in financing North Korea's unlawful weapons programs. These Australian sanctions aim to disrupt North Korea's illicit revenue-generating networks, particularly those using fraudulent IT workers to raise funds for the regime's weapons programs, and reinforce international efforts to pressure North Korea to comply with its international obligations.
articles.source: Consilium.europa.eu / Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade / ACAMS

articles.headline: OCC Releases October 2026 Enforcement Actions, Citing BSA/AML Deficiencies at Major Banks
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant deficiencies in Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance programs at major national banks. These actions are intended to compel boards of directors and management to address and correct identified violations and deficient practices.

Among the actions, American Express National Bank in Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs. Bank of America, N.A., based in Charlotte, North Carolina, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties: Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds. These individual actions underscore the OCC's focus on accountability for misconduct within financial institutions.

articles.headline: OCC Report Finds Nine Major Banks Engaged in Debanking Practices
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on October 14, 2026, titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' which concludes that nine of the largest national banks it supervises maintained policies or practices that may have led to the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The report examined nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 50,000 documents from banks between 2020 and September 2025.

The OCC identified two broad categories of policies presenting an elevated risk of influencing banks to deny services: general reputation risk policies and industry-specific policies. Industry-specific restrictions included those on Arctic oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms, detention facilities, tobacco, and digital asset activities.

While the OCC did not announce any immediate enforcement actions or penalties in this report, Comptroller Jonathan Gould stated that the agency would be assessing further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework for large banks. The OCC is also considering actions to prevent discrimination based on political or religious beliefs and to address the role of reputation risk in bank decision-making.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
